quartiers:Kastella / Profitis Ilias.name: Kastella / Profitis Ilias
quartiers:Kastella / Profitis Ilias.teaser: Villas stepped up the old acropolis of Munichia, with the whole gulf laid out at the top
quartiers:Kastella / Profitis Ilias.story: Kastella is the hill the ancients called Munichia, about 87 metres of rock rising straight off the water between Mikrolimano and Zea. Piraeans split it in two names: Kastella for the slope that looks at the sea, Profitis Ilias for the landward crown. In 1875 the architect Ernst Ziller bought land on Plateia Alexandras and built the row still called Ziller's neighbourhood; neoclassical and interwar villas followed, dropping in terraces and stairways toward the harbour. It is now the most sought-after address in the port, quiet stepped lanes where the late sun turns the old facades gold and the only noise is a scooter labouring uphill.
quartiers:Kastella / Profitis Ilias.why: Climb it for the stairways and the evening light; it is a residential hill that goes to bed early, not a scene.

quartiers:Mikrolimano / Munichia.name: Mikrolimano / Munichia
quartiers:Mikrolimano / Munichia.teaser: The smallest ancient war harbour, now a horseshoe of masts and fish tables: choose by name
quartiers:Mikrolimano / Munichia.story: Munichia was the smallest of the three ancient war harbours of Piraeus, and its Ottoman-era name, Tourkolimano, held until 1967, when it was renamed Mikrolimano, the little harbour. After the 1922 catastrophe refugees from Asia Minor threw up shacks along its shore; the first grand psarotavernes arrived around 1960 and the quay has fed Athens fish ever since. Tonight it is a tight crescent of sailing-club dinghies, fishing caiques and tablecloths a step from the water, with a waiter at almost every door calling to passers-by. Some of the most serious fish kitchens in Greece share this quay with places that sell nothing but the view.
quartiers:Mikrolimano / Munichia.why: Book a named house before you arrive: a tout at the door is the surest sign you are at the wrong table.

quartiers:Pasalimani / Zea.name: Pasalimani / Zea
quartiers:Pasalimani / Zea.teaser: The round middle harbour where Piraeus takes its evening walk
quartiers:Pasalimani / Zea.story: Zea is the near-circular basin between Kastella and the Piraiki peninsula, and in antiquity it was the largest of Athens's three war harbours; the name is traced to zea, a fine grain. The Ottomans called it Pasalimani, the pasha's harbour, and most Piraeans still do. Today it is Marina Zeas: charter yachts and superyachts swinging on their lines, gangways down, crews at work on the decks, and a ring of cafés and cocktail bars facing them across the quay. This is where the city does its volta, families in the early evening, the café crowd later, and on a weekend the terraces still full near midnight.
quartiers:Pasalimani / Zea.why: Take an evening drink facing the boats, then walk the whole circle once the heat lifts.
facts: The evening volta and the café terraces round the basin

quartiers:Piraiki / Akti Themistokleous.name: Piraiki / Akti Themistokleous
quartiers:Piraiki / Akti Themistokleous.teaser: The west-facing tip of the peninsula: swimming rocks, ancient wall blocks and the sun dropping into the gulf
quartiers:Piraiki / Akti Themistokleous.story: Piraiki is the rocky south-western end of the Piraeus peninsula, one long shore road, Akti Themistokleous, running past flat swimming rocks, small coves and low houses. Along the waterline Konon's 4th-century-BC fortification surfaces in courses of squared stone. All summer locals spread towels on the rock and go in from the ledges. The state has funded a €25m coastal promenade here from the Recovery Fund, with a walkway and lighting for the Cononian wall; the official timetable ran to December 2025, but its progress could not be confirmed in October 2026, so expect works in places.
quartiers:Piraiki / Akti Themistokleous.why: Be on the rocks for the last hour of light: the whole shore faces west and the locals know it.

quartiers:Freattyda.name: Freattyda
quartiers:Freattyda.teaser: A small shore quarter named for one of the strangest courts of ancient Athens
quartiers:Freattyda.story: Freattyda is the compact quarter on the south-eastern lip of the peninsula, just below Zea, where the marina promenade turns toward the open Piraiki coast. It carries the name of Phreattys, a court with one peculiar rule: a man already exiled for an unintentional killing, and then accused of another, could not set foot on Attic soil, so he pleaded his case from a boat while the judges sat on the shore. The waterline here was reshaped in the 1960s and the quarter today is quiet and residential, a few tavernas on Leoforos Freattydos and a small municipal beach in the rebuilt cove.
quartiers:Freattyda.why: Use it as the turning point: a swim in the cove, then walk west along Piraiki as the light drops.

quartiers:Terpsithea.name: Terpsithea
quartiers:Terpsithea.teaser: The big square where the two spine avenues cross, and where Piraeus simply goes about its day
quartiers:Terpsithea.story: Terpsithea is named for the large square at the crossing of the city's two spine avenues: Iroon Polytechneiou, climbing toward Hatzikyriakeio, and 2as Merarchias, running from the central port down to Zea. The plateia covers roughly 20 stremmata, about two hectares, and splits into four smaller squares, each with its own benches, kiosks and regulars. The blocks around it are ordinary residential Piraeus: kafeneia with men over backgammon, bakeries, neighbourhood tavernas cooking for people who live upstairs. There is no view and no monument to tick off, which is the reason to come: this is the port as its own residents use it.
quartiers:Terpsithea.why: Sit an hour in one of the four squares on a weekday and watch the city be a city.

quartiers:Kentro & the Central Port / Ti.name: Kentro & the Central Port / Tinaneios
quartiers:Kentro & the Central Port / Ti.teaser: Ferry gates, the 1869 railway terminus and a shaded garden laid out in 1854
quartiers:Kentro & the Central Port / Ti.story: This is the working heart most travellers only cross on the way to a boat. The Kantharos commercial harbour, the Aegean ferry gates and the terminus of Greece's oldest railway, the Athens–Piraeus line of 1869, now metro line 1, all meet at Plateia Karaiskaki. For centuries sailors knew the place as Porto Leone, after a marble lion that guarded the harbour until the Venetians shipped it to Venice in 1687. A block inland the Tinaneios Garden, laid out in 1854 under the French admiral de Tinan, gives a rare patch of shade among the shipping offices, with the ship horns still audible through the trees.
quartiers:Kentro & the Central Port / Ti.why: Treat it as your arrival ritual: a coffee before the crowds, then provisions, then the boat.

quartiers:Nikaia / Kokkinia.name: Nikaia / Kokkinia
quartiers:Nikaia / Kokkinia.teaser: The great refugee town of 1923, its streets named for the lost cities of Asia Minor
quartiers:Nikaia / Kokkinia.story: When well over a million Greeks were driven out of Asia Minor after 1922, Nea Kokkinia was founded here in 1923, and by the 1928 census it held 33,000 people, the most populous refugee settlement of all. Its grid was named street by street for the cities they had lost: Smyrnis, Aidiniou, Attaleias, Kaisareias. In August 1944 the occupiers sealed the district and rounded up its men in the blockade remembered as Bloody Kokkinia, and the anniversary is still marked. The church of Osia Xeni anchors the centre. Now the town of Nikaia, it keeps the Mikrasiatika kitchen alive and sees almost no tourists.
quartiers:Nikaia / Kokkinia.why: Walk the street names as a map of what was lost, then eat what the refugees brought with them.

quartiers:Drapetsona.name: Drapetsona
quartiers:Drapetsona.teaser: The refugee shanty town of a famous song, its fertiliser-works shore opened as a park
quartiers:Drapetsona.story: West of the central port lies the other great refugee quarter: after 1922 the largest shanty settlement in Attica, 36,485 people by the 1928 census, living off the shipyards and above all the Lipasmata fertiliser works. Its smoke and hardship became one of Greece's defining songs, 'Drapetsona', by Mikis Theodorakis and Tasos Livaditis, sung by Grigoris Bithikotsis around 1960. The works shut in 1999 and part of the poisoned shore is now a seafront park; the rest of the vast site is still argued over, with a state plan for an innovation centre and court challenges unresolved. Still working-class, its tables are among the most honest near the port.
quartiers:Drapetsona.why: Go for the sunset over the old works' quay, then dinner on the kebab row.

walks:The Kastella–Mikrolimano loop.name: The Kastella–Mikrolimano loop
walks:The Kastella–Mikrolimano loop.teaser: Round the fishing harbour, then up the stairways of the amphitheatre above it
walks:The Kastella–Mikrolimano loop.story: Start on the quay of Mikrolimano, the ancient Munichia, whose harbour goddess was Artemis Munichia; more than eighty ship-houses once lined the basin where the fish restaurants now set their tables. Walk the crescent first, past the yacht-club slips, then turn uphill into Kastella, where lanes become flights of steps between villas and the theatre of ancient Munichia once looked down on the harbour. About twenty minutes of climbing and the whole Saronic lies flat below you, Mikrolimano shrunk to a ring of masts. Come down by another stair and finish back at the water as the lamps come on.
walks:The Kastella–Mikrolimano loop.why: Reach the top at sunset and come down to the harbour in the blue hour.

walks:The Zea (Pasalimani) marina round.name: The Zea (Pasalimani) marina round
walks:The Zea (Pasalimani) marina round.teaser: A flat circuit of a round ancient war harbour, superyachts where triremes once dried
walks:The Zea (Pasalimani) marina round.story: Zea held the largest share of Athens's war fleet: about 196 ship-houses ran round this basin, sloping stone ramps where triremes were hauled out to dry, and their remains still lie under the quays, roads and apartment blocks you walk past. Go round in the morning, when the marina is at work: crews washing down decks, provisioning vans at the gangways, café terraces being set. Halfway round, a ground-floor window lets you peer down at three of those ancient ramps. Back at the Hellenic Maritime Museum you have read two and a half thousand years of the same shoreline in one easy circle.
walks:The Zea (Pasalimani) marina round.why: Walk it slowly before noon and look down, not up: the ancient harbour is under your feet.

walks:Up Profitis Ilias to the Veakeio.name: Up Profitis Ilias to the Veakeio
walks:Up Profitis Ilias to the Veakeio.teaser: The city's balcony: the old acropolis of Munichia, with an open-air theatre cut into its slope
walks:Up Profitis Ilias to the Veakeio.story: The summit of Profitis Ilias was the acropolis of ancient Munichia, and in 403 BC the democrats under Thrasybulus held this height and beat the forces of the Thirty Tyrants on its slope, the fight that restored democracy to Athens. Today the crown is a church terrace and the Veakeio's open-air seats, and from about 87 metres you take in the central port, Zea, Mikrolimano and the islands of the Saronic in a single turn of the head. On summer nights the hill fills with theatregoers; out of season, and at midday, you will likely have the terrace to yourself and the wind.
walks:Up Profitis Ilias to the Veakeio.why: Climb for the last half hour before sunset, then stay if the Veakeio has a show that night.

walks:The Piraiki coast walk to the ligh.name: The Piraiki coast walk to the lighthouse
walks:The Piraiki coast walk to the ligh.teaser: Along the line of the ancient sea wall to the lighthouse at the tip
walks:The Piraiki coast walk to the ligh.story: The shore road follows the line of the sea wall Themistocles began and Konon rebuilt in the 4th century BC, and in places the surf still breaks over its cut blocks. Midway the shore opens at Aphrodite cove, Baikoutsi to locals, under a tall concrete cross and a whitewashed island-style chapel. Near the tip, by the lighthouse, rock-cut remains have long been pointed out as the Tomb of Themistocles, an identification no one has proved. Walk it in the long light before dusk, with ships for Aegina and Salamina crossing the gulf ahead of you, and expect sections under promenade works.
walks:The Piraiki coast walk to the ligh.why: Set off about 90 minutes before sunset so you reach the tip as the sun goes down.

walks:The Hippodamian grid & the Eetione.name: The Hippodamian grid & the Eetioneia Gate walls
walks:The Hippodamian grid & the Eetione.teaser: The largest walkable stretch of the port's ancient walls, looking down on the ferries
walks:The Hippodamian grid & the Eetione.story: In the mid-5th century BC Hippodamus of Miletus, the man Aristotle credits with inventing town planning, laid Piraeus out on a rational grid, and the walls begun under Themistocles wrapped it in stone. On the Kastraki knoll of the western arm, in 411 BC, the oligarchs of the Four Hundred fortified the Eetioneia point, and its gate stands on the largest walkable stretch of the circuit. Floodlit since January 2024, the site was enlarged in April 2026 with about seven stremmata handed over by the port authority, facing the National Museum of Underwater Antiquities now being built. Below you, the ferries load for the islands.
walks:The Hippodamian grid & the Eetione.why: Come in the morning and stand on the wall line: ancient gate behind you, island ferries at your feet.

walks:The central-port arcades & the Mun.name: The central-port arcades & the Municipal Theatre
walks:The central-port arcades & the Mun.teaser: From the 1895 theatre through market arcades to the water: the port centre on foot
walks:The central-port arcades & the Mun.story: Start under the Corinthian portico of the Municipal Theatre on Korai Square, opened in 1895 and told in its own card, and walk down through the belle-époque blocks of the centre, whose streets still keep to the ancient planned lines. Turn into the arcades off Gounari, where the stoa kafeneia pour briki coffee for market porters, then work the two blocks round the Agia Triada market, where Armenian and Asia Minor houses still cure pastourma and roast nuts. Finish at the water by Agios Spyridon, where on 6 January a cross is thrown into the central harbour and swimmers dive for it. Expect traffic between the stops.

calas:Votsalakia Municipal Beach.name: Votsalakia Municipal Beach
calas:Votsalakia Municipal Beach.teaser: The town's own pebble beach, start line of an 1896 Olympic swim revived in 2025
calas:Votsalakia Municipal Beach.story: Votsalakia means little pebbles: a free municipal strip of pebble and coarse sand under the tiers of Kastella, between Zea and Mikrolimano, looking out at the low islet of Koumoundourou. It is one of the old coves of Piraeus and a listed archaeological site. After storm damage in 2021 the municipality rebuilt the sports side with five new courts, five-a-side, tennis and beach volley, and each summer sets up a Seatrac, a solar-powered rail seat beside the lifeguard post that lets wheelchair users enter the sea unaided. On 6 September 2025 swimmers pushed off here for Pier K of Zea, reviving the course of the 1896 Olympic open-water swim. In winter it belongs to the year-round plungers.
calas:Votsalakia Municipal Beach.why: Swim early on a calm summer morning when it has not rained for days.

calas:Freattyda Municipal Beach.name: Freattyda Municipal Beach
calas:Freattyda Municipal Beach.teaser: A built city strip at the mouth of Zea, the one Piraeus swim the state monitors
calas:Freattyda Municipal Beach.story: When Zea marina was dug out in the early 1960s, the old Freattyda cove disappeared and this artificial strip of roughly 400 metres was built in its place, at the marina's mouth beside the Hellenic Maritime Museum. It has been a designated EU bathing water since 1990 and the state rates it suitable, though its own profile grades the water only moderate and names the marina as a pollution source. The environmental group PAKOE, which in past seasons contradicted the state, sampled two points here on 4 May 2026 and rated both suitable. In summer there are lifeguards and sunbeds; at dawn the water is glassy and nearly empty.

calas:Ormos Afroditis (Aphrodite Cove) r.name: Ormos Afroditis (Aphrodite Cove) rocks
calas:Ormos Afroditis (Aphrodite Cove) r.teaser: Flat rock under a seamen's cross: the most local swim in the port
calas:Ormos Afroditis (Aphrodite Cove) r.story: There is no beach here, only flat rock on the Piraiki shore, a concrete cross and the blue-domed chapel of Agios Nikolaos, patron of sailors. Locals call the spot o Stavros, the cross, for the Monument of the Unknown Sailor raised on 7 December 1969, and underfoot lie fallen stones of the Cononian wall. At Epiphany the waters are blessed here as well. The state lists no bathing water at this point and PAKOE has flagged it among the worst on the peninsula, yet the neighbourhood swims it anyway, on calm days after a dry spell, stepping carefully round the sea urchins.
calas:Ormos Afroditis (Aphrodite Cove) r.why: Swim it only on a still day after a dry week; otherwise come for the sunset and keep your feet dry.

calas:Batis Beach.name: Batis Beach
calas:Batis Beach.teaser: The nearest real sand east of the port, shallow, free and on the coastal tram
calas:Batis Beach.story: Batis is the first proper sand beach east of Piraeus, on the Palaio Faliro shore: shallow, warm water, a palm-lined promenade behind, and both free stretches and an organised section with sunbeds. It is on coastal tram line 7, which since February 2026 runs from Akti Poseidonos in the port along the shore toward Voula, and the stop is named Batis, a stop beyond Flisvos. The state rates the water suitable, and PAKOE's 2026 sampling also rated Batis suitable, after it had flagged the beach in 2025. Cleaner than the Piraiki rocks, though it is still city water, not island-clear.

culture:Archaeological Museum of Piraeus.name: Archaeological Museum of Piraeus
culture:Archaeological Museum of Piraeus.teaser: Four Classical bronzes in one room, found in 1959 by workmen digging a sewer
culture:Archaeological Museum of Piraeus.story: In July 1959 a crew laying a sewer where Georgiou A' meets Filonos hit a bronze hand about a metre and a half down. Beneath it lay four statues packed in ash, with a coin of 87/86 BC, most likely loot crated for Sulla's ships after his army stormed Athens and Piraeus in 86 BC and never sailed. They stand together now: the Piraeus Apollo, the oldest large hollow-cast bronze known, beside a helmeted Athena and two Artemis. The two-storey building wraps the ruined Hellenistic theatre of Zea, and the ten rooms run on to the Kallithea funerary monument and Minoan and Mycenaean figurines.

culture:Zea Shipsheds (ancient neosoikoi.name: Zea Shipsheds (ancient neosoikoi)
culture:Zea Shipsheds (ancient neosoikoi.teaser: Slipways that may have held the Salamis triremes, seen through an apartment-block window
culture:Zea Shipsheds (ancient neosoikoi.story: The yachts of Pasalimani float over the ground where Athens kept its war fleet. Divers and excavators of the Zea Harbour Project, led by Bjørn Lovén for the Danish Institute at Athens, carbon-dated shipshed timbers to roughly 520-480 BC, which puts these stone ramps in service when the triremes rowed out to Salamis in 480. Close to four hundred sheds once lined the three harbours of Piraeus. The surviving slipways are walled into the basement of a modern block, lit by whatever daylight slides through a ground-floor window. There is no ticket and no door: you bend down on the pavement and look in.
culture:Zea Shipsheds (ancient neosoikoi.why: It is the nearest you can stand to the fleet that won Salamis, and it costs nothing but a crouch.

culture:Hellenic Maritime Museum.name: Hellenic Maritime Museum
culture:Hellenic Maritime Museum.teaser: Ship models and naval history built around a stretch of the ancient sea-wall, a submarine tower outside
culture:Hellenic Maritime Museum.story: When the museum moved into its building on the Zea quay in 1971 it kept what was in the ground. A length of the port's fortification runs through the halls: the wall Themistocles began after Salamis and Konon rebuilt in the 4th century BC, after Sparta had made Athens tear it down. Around it hang ship models, figureheads, charts and the paintings of Greek sea battles. On the quay outside stands the conning tower of the Second World War submarine Papanikolis, a grey steel lump among the white yachts. The collection is about ships; the building is part of the wall that once kept them safe.

culture:Municipal Theatre of Piraeus.teaser: A neoclassical theatre of 1895 that kept its original wooden stage
culture:Municipal Theatre of Piraeus.story: The Piraeus architect Ioannis Lazarimos laid the foundation stone in 1884, and the house opened on 9 April 1895 behind a portico of Corinthian columns on Korai Square, the shipowners' city showing Athens what it could build. After about a decade shut, restoration between 2008 and 2013 reopened it on 22 October 2013 and exposed the 1895 wooden stage, one of the few of its age still in use in Europe. Inside it is red velvet, gilt boxes and a painted ceiling. It is a working theatre, not a daytime monument: you see it by buying a seat or joining a scheduled tour.

culture:Veakeio Municipal Theatre.name: Veakeio Municipal Theatre
culture:Veakeio Municipal Theatre.teaser: Two thousand open-air seats on Profitis Ilias, the Saronic Gulf behind the stage
culture:Veakeio Municipal Theatre.story: The amphitheatre was poured in concrete in 1969, under the colonels, and named the Skylitseio; it opened with Verdi's Nabucco. In 1976, with democracy restored, the city renamed it for Emilios Veakis, the Piraeus-born tragic actor whose left-wing politics had cost him dearly after the war. Two thousand seats climb the hill about 87 metres above the sea, and on a summer night the ferries' lights slide across the gulf behind the performers. The 2026 season ran pop and Greek song into late September, with Helena Paparizou on 7 September and Michalis Hatzigiannis on 26 September. Seats are bare stone and the climb is steep.

His designs show whole operas as painted rooms: towers, temples and storm skies, drawn for a stage in Berlin and hung here a short walk from the market.

culture:Cine Melina.story: Drapetsona began as the tents and shacks of Asia Minor refugees in 1922, pitched beside the Lipasmata fertiliser works, and for decades its name meant acrid air and hard lives. Its summer cinema is a walled courtyard of climbing vines and folding chairs, with tickets priced for the neighbourhood and some tribute nights free. craft:I Anemi — the rope-house.name: I Anemi — the rope-house
craft:I Anemi — the rope-house.teaser: The Kordoni family's rope shop, where three-strand line is still cut to your length
craft:I Anemi — the rope-house.story: An anemi is the big reel on which rope was twisted, and the shop carries the name. The Kordoni family began spinning rope by hand in 1936 for the busiest port in Greece, opened this counter in 1970, and by 1990 the third generation had added brass fittings, fenders and life-rings. Their surname, fittingly, sounds like the Greek for cord. Three-strand rope still comes off the reel and is measured and cut across the counter while you wait. This is a working chandlery for boatmen, Greek-first and busiest early on weekdays, with nothing made to be browsed.

craft:Banks Sails Greece.name: Banks Sails Greece
craft:Banks Sails Greece.teaser: A working sail loft above the fishing harbour, run by twins who race what they cut
craft:Banks Sails Greece.story: It began in 1987 as Yacht-Care Sailmakers: two racing sailors, Spyros and Dimitris, and a few sewing machines over Mikrolimano. In 2008 the loft joined the Italian Banks Sails network and began making sails for yachts up to 141 feet. In 2020 Spyros's twin sons, George and Stratis, both ranked racers, took it over, so the people cutting the cloth also race on it. Besides sails they make biminis, sprayhoods and stackpacks, and measure for ORCi and IRC certificates. Nothing is sold off a shelf: it is a made-to-measure loft, and you ring before you climb the stairs.

craft:No class to enrol in.name: No class to enrol in
craft:No class to enrol in.teaser: Piraeus keeps its rope and sail trades working, but neither runs a course you can sign up for
craft:No class to enrol in.story: We looked for a craft class in Piraeus and did not find one to recommend. The rope-house and the sail loft are working businesses that serve boats, not workshops that teach visitors, and we found no course, open day or demonstration at either. What you can do is real enough: buy three-strand rope cut to length across a counter that has sold it since 1970, or bring a damaged sail to a loft whose owners race on what they make. Treat both as errands for the boat, done in Greek and on their hours, and you will see the trade as it actually runs.

Greek coffee arrives in a small cup under a thick skin of kaimaki, and at breakfast it sits beside fried smelt on a tin plate, among porters, fishmongers and sailors off the boats. LiFO counted it in 2019 among the old kafeneia the port still keeps. Come early, speak a few words of Greek, and leave the phone in your pocket.

coffee-gardens:O Stamatis.teaser: A kafeneio with its 1935 operating licence framed on the wall; phone before you go
coffee-gardens:O Stamatis.story: On Leocharous, in the lanes behind the Municipal Market, this kafeneio-ouzeri still hangs its original 1935 operating licence on the wall. Coffee is boiled in a briki and served on marble to regulars who have sat in the same chairs for half a century. coffee-gardens:Möte.name: Möte
coffee-gardens:Möte.teaser: Single-origin coffee in a high-ceilinged 1936 corner room on Sotiros Dios
coffee-gardens:Möte.story: Möte takes its beans from the team of Stefanos Domatiotis, who won the World Brewers Cup in 2014, and pours them in a 1936 corner building on Sotiros Dios, with tall windows and a ceiling high enough to keep the room quiet. It is coffee-first and unhurried in a town where the default is a frappé on a harbour terrace. The pour-over is the point: an Ethiopian like the Buki comes out floral and almost as clear as tea. Of the cafés in this section it is the one where you can open a laptop and stay a while.

The room is a real daytime place to work: steady, quiet and unhurried. There is no sea view and no terrace, and it closes in the late afternoon.

gastronomy:Ichthyoskala Keratsiniou.teaser: The night's Aegean catch, sung off by the crate under floodlights before most of Piraeus wakes
gastronomy:Ichthyoskala Keratsiniou.story: Since 1965 the fish of half the Aegean has come ashore at Limani Irakleiou, on the Keratsini edge of the port, and the old guide calls it the largest auction in Greece. Trawlers and small gri-gri purse-seiners moor under floodlights after midnight; auctioneers call prices over stacked crates of red mullet, gavros, cuttlefish and squid, and the buyers for the port's tavernas and the Athens fishmongers settle it all before sunrise. Arrive at mid-morning and all that is left is a hosed concrete floor and gulls. This is a working quay, not a food hall.

After 1922 refugees from Smyrna and Anatolia filled this quarter with their shopfronts and three rows of fish stalls, and on Gounari and Tsamadou their trades still run within about 200 metres of each other: cured beef, pastry sheets, roasted nuts, spices from open sacks. Each of those counters has its own card below. Come on foot, on a weekday morning.

gastronomy:Avakian.teaser: Cappadocian pastourma cured by one Armenian family since 1922, in an arcade off Gounari
gastronomy:Avakian.story: Aram Avakian came from Kaisareia in Cappadocia to Palia Kokkinia in 1922 and cured his first pastourma on his own rooftop before taking a market stall; his son Giorgos carried the craft on, and Athens Voice notes the shop now trades as 'O Giorgos' while everyone still says Avakian. The family moved into the Stoa Politou arcade when the old market came down in 1967. The beef is air-cured under a red crust of fenugreek and garlic, sold beside spicy soutzouki and kavourma. gastronomy:Mandragoras.teaser: Open sacks of mountain oregano and Greek saffron, weighed out on Gounari since 1963
gastronomy:Mandragoras.story: Fotis Vasilopoulos began working at eight, in a grocery in Nafplio, and opened Mandragoras in 1955; it has occupied its spot on Gounari since 1963. around:Aegina.name: Aegina
around:Aegina.teaser: Forty minutes on a fast boat to the pistachio island and a Doric temple on a pine hill
around:Aegina.story: Aegina is the nearest real island, with boats from Piraeus through the day. In late August its orchards start their pistachio harvest; the nut has been protected as Fistiki Aiginis since the 1990s and growers have pooled their crop in a cooperative since 1947. The temple of Aphaia, on the far side of the island, went up around 500 to 490 BC, Doric, on a pine hill about 160 metres up, some 15 km from the harbour town. Take the bus or a taxi out, then come back to the port for an ouzo with a bag of the year's nuts.

around:Salamina.story: The small car ferries shuttling between Perama and Paloukia cross the narrows where the Greek triremes broke the Persian fleet in September 480 BC. On the island, the Kynosoura peninsula south of the port holds the burial mound of the Salamis dead and a view straight back over the strait. Further south, near Peristeria, is the cave where Euripides is said to have written; excavators found a fifth-century BC cup there with his name on it.

around:Hydra.name: Hydra
around:Hydra.teaser: No cars, no scooters, not even bicycles: just stone, mules and water taxis
around:Hydra.story: Local law keeps every motor vehicle off Hydra apart from the refuse and fire trucks and the ambulance, and a rule from the 1950s keeps bicycles off too. So the cargo from the boat goes up the stepped lanes on donkeys and mules, and the coast is served by water taxis. From the harbour, walk west from it past the small pebble beach at Avlaki to Kamini, a fishing harbour with tavernas and swimming rocks; past Kamini the way becomes a partly cobbled coastal path toward Vlychos. bars:Istioploikos.teaser: A two-level deck at the tip of Mikrolimano, the sailboats moored right under the rail
bars:Istioploikos.story: Mikrolimano was Mounichia, one of the war harbours of Themistocles' Athens; today its curved quay holds the yacht basin, and Istioploikos, 'the yachtsman', has held its tip since 1997. It stands a little apart from the row of fish terraces, a two-deck building that looks like a small liner about to cast off. The café side runs from the morning; the bar and kitchen take over late, and a DJ plays on Sunday afternoons. As the light goes, the ouzo turns cloudy over ice and a whole grilled tsipoura or fangri comes to the rail, the masts knocking below.

The day starts with brunch at weekends, poached eggs on sando bread, pancakes, a club sandwich, and ends with cocktails as the caiques' lights come on. People come for the deck and the sunset more than for the mixing.

bars:801 Rooftop Bar.teaser: Eight floors up, level with the cranes and the night ferries of the Great Harbour
bars:801 Rooftop Bar.story: Spyros Metaxa built his first distillery in Piraeus in 1888, and the brandy was made in the port until 1968, when the company moved to Kifissia. Converting the waterfront building into the Mitsis N'U hotel in 2024, Divercity Architects kept the shapes of the barrels in wooden arches and amber light. The 801 is on the eighth floor at Aristidou 16–20, opposite Gate E7, and you drink eye-level with the gantries as the night boats back out for the islands. The list leans Greek: Liminality builds reposado tequila and Metaxa 12 with chamomile, mustard seed and pink grapefruit.

bars:Paléo.name: Paléo
bars:Paléo.teaser: Two to three hundred obscure southern-European labels in a Retsina-quarter warehouse
bars:Paléo.story: The quarter is called Retsina, the port's old tobacco-warehouse grid, inland and with no view, and Paléo fills one of those warehouses at Polydeukous 39. The sommelier-owner Yannis Kaimenakis travels the south of Europe for small wineries few people have heard of, two to three hundred labels in all, and prices them close to retail on principle, which in a port of marina markups is a stand. The by-the-glass list can change daily. Let him choose, and order pasta e fagioli or the Tuscan chicken-liver pâté to keep the bottle company.

bars:Méthe.teaser: Forty labels reaching Austria and Georgia, and 48-hour pizza, on the ferry avenue
bars:Méthe.story: Méthe is the Greek word for wine's euphoric drunkenness, and the bar that took the name opened on 2 January 2026 at Akti Miaouli 73, facing the blue-domed church of Agios Nikolaos, patron of sailors. bars:Amsterdam Bar.story: Dimitris Doumakis opened the place in 2008 as O'Canto, then renamed it Amsterdam to bring a piece of the Dutch capital to Pasalimani. bars:Retsina — the port's wine.name: Retsina — the port's wine
bars:Retsina — the port's wine.teaser: Savatiano with Aleppo-pine resin in the ferment: the white the port has drunk with fried fish for a century
bars:Retsina — the port's wine.story: Retsina is the one wine here that can claim to be local. It is mostly Savatiano, sometimes with a splash of Roditis, and Aleppo-pine resin goes into the must while it ferments, which gives the pine note. It is not a PDO but a traditional appellation, an OKP, belonging to the Mesogeia plain east of Athens, close enough for the port to call it its own; its vineyards belong to the Athens guide. In Piraeus it comes cold, in a tin jug or a short bottle, beside the fried fish. The barrel version poured in Agios Dionysios has its own card in the tables: To Eidikon.
bars:Retsina — the port's wine.why: Drink it very cold with something fried and salty; that is the job it was made for.

bars:Ouzo with the fried fish.name: Ouzo with the fried fish
bars:Ouzo with the fried fish.teaser: Anise that turns milk-white on ice, a karafaki at a time, and the small fried fish that slow it down
bars:Ouzo with the fried fish.story: At the ouzeri the drink is the point and the food comes to keep you there. Ouzo is an anise-flavoured grape spirit; drop in ice or water and it clouds white, the louche, as the anise oils come out of solution. Its geographical indication is reserved to Greece and Cyprus, and its home is Plomari on Lesvos, not this quay. Tsipouro is the rougher cousin, distilled from the skins and stems left after pressing, usually without anise; in Crete the same idea is tsikoudia, called raki. Neither was born here. Both are what the port pours, with fried gavros, lemon and a few mezedes.
bars:Ouzo with the fried fish.why: Order a karafaki, add ice yourself, and wait for the fish: ouzo is drunk with food, never alone.
facts: Clear until the ice goes in, then milk-white, anise on the nose

listening:Rebetiko was born here.name: Rebetiko was born here
listening:Rebetiko was born here.teaser: The Greek urban blues took its classic shape on these docks after 1922
listening:Rebetiko was born here.story: Rebetiko, the Greek urban blues, took its classic bouzouki-led shape in working-class Piraeus in the 1920s and 30s, in the tekedes, the hashish dens, of Drapetsona, Agios Dionysios and the Lemonadika fruit market by Karaiskaki Square, as refugees from the 1922 Asia Minor catastrophe crowded the port. The bouzouki and the baglamas came ashore on the same quays as the ouzo and the meze. Under the Metaxas regime, in power from August 1936, the songs were censored and the hashish lyrics cut. The music survived. UNESCO inscribed rebetiko on its intangible-heritage list in December 2017.
listening:Rebetiko was born here.why: Hear it in a room in the quarters it came from, not in a show staged for a tour bus.
facts: Propolemikon in Agios Dionysios, where the old quartet played, and Revaizi on the Drapetsona edge; both are in this guide
Athens and Piraeus both claim the cradle, and the Smyrna café style and the Piraeus bouzouki style are told as rival roots; the UNESCO entry speaks of urban working-class people, not of one quarter

listening:The Famous Quartet of Piraeus.name: The Famous Quartet of Piraeus — 1934
listening:The Famous Quartet of Piraeus.teaser: Four players, two bouzoukis, a baglamas and a voice: the first band of its kind
listening:The Famous Quartet of Piraeus.story: In 1934 Markos Vamvakaris, Giorgos Batis, Anestis Delias and Stratos Pagioumtzis began playing together as «Η τετράς η ξακουστή του Πειραιώς», the Famous Quartet of Piraeus: two bouzoukis, a baglamas and singing, the first group made of bouzouki and baglamas specialists. Batis gave it the grand name; he had run his own café in the port since 1931. None of the four was born in Piraeus. In 1935 they recorded «Φραγκοσυριανή» (Frangosyriani) together. The Metaxas regime's censorship broke the run within a few years.
listening:The Famous Quartet of Piraeus.why: Put on a 1930s recording of the four before you go to a rebetadiko; you will hear where every band since comes from.
facts: Propolemikon in Agios Dionysios, which keeps the quartet in its house history; its own card is in the tables

listening:Bayanteras — the one rebetis b.name: Bayanteras — a son of the port
listening:Bayanteras — the one rebetis b.teaser: He came from Piraeus itself, and gave his own back-street quarter a song
listening:Bayanteras — the one rebetis b.story: Dimitris Gogos, known as Bayanteras (1903–1985), was born in Piraeus on 28 February 1903, in the working-class quarter of Hatzikyriakio. That sets him apart: the founding quartet were islanders and refugees who came ashore, and none was a native. He became one of rebetiko's most influential singers and composers. The nickname is tied to Kálmán's operetta Die Bajadere, which by the usual account he arranged for bouzouki around 1925. In 1938 he wrote «Χατζηκυριάκειο», putting the name of his home quarter into the songbook.
listening:Bayanteras — the one rebetis b.why: Walk Hatzikyriakio with «Χατζηκυριάκειο» in your ears; the song is about the streets around you.

listening:Revaizi.name: Revaizi
listening:Revaizi.teaser: A live kompania three nights a week, on the ground where the tekedes stood
listening:Revaizi.story: Revaizi, at Thermopylon 28 on the Drapetsona side of the port, is a mezedopoleio with bouzouki in the quarter where the hashish dens once stood. A full kompania plays Friday, Saturday and Sunday, and the regulars sing along. The kitchen is Cretan rather than Asia Minor: chochlioi, snails fried with rosemary, a risotto with apaki, the smoked Cretan pork, and raki in small bottles. Come as much for the room and the raki as for the set list. It is out toward Drapetsona, a taxi ride rather than a walk from the cruise gates.

listening:Stou Thoma & To Palio Roloi.teaser: Two central rooms where the regulars, not a tour group, get up to dance the zeibekiko
listening:Stou Thoma & To Palio Roloi.story: Two rooms in the town centre keep live rebetiko away from the waterfront. Stou Thoma, at Mavromichali 22–24 in Agia Sofia, sits in an arcade that was once the ticket entrance of an open-air cinema; the kompania plays Wednesday to Saturday from about ten at night. To Palio Roloi, at Dimosthenous 5 beside the covered market, is in old Troumba, the sailors' quarter of Never on Sunday, and its band starts on Friday and Saturday afternoons around five, when the regulars get up for the zeibekiko. Both change their hours.

It is not a daytime café or a place to work: it is a warm room for after dark.

listening:Ta Paidia tou Pirea — 1960.name: 'Ta Paidia tou Pirea' — 1960
listening:Ta Paidia tou Pirea — 1960.teaser: A song about the boys of Piraeus, shot on these quays, won an Oscar in 1961
listening:Ta Paidia tou Pirea — 1960.story: «Τα Παιδιά του Πειραιά», music by Manos Hadjidakis, sung by Melina Mercouri as Ilya in Jules Dassin's «Ποτέ την Κυριακή», Never on Sunday, was set and filmed in the port in 1960. On 17 April 1961 it won the Academy Award for Best Original Song, the first winner in a language other than English. Hadjidakis stayed away from the ceremony. The tune went round the world in English with words by Billy Towne, which were not the ones heard in the film. The Greek lyric never mentions Sunday; the title was the film's.
listening:Ta Paidia tou Pirea — 1960.why: Watch the film before you come, then walk the Troumba streets and the quays it was shot on.

listening:Hi-fi — honestly.name: Hi-fi — honestly
listening:Hi-fi — honestly.teaser: No hi-fi listening bar in Piraeus this guide can vouch for; the real listening here has no speakers
listening:Hi-fi — honestly.story: A listening bar is a room where the sound system and the records are the point and the drinks come second. An October 2026 search found none in Piraeus confirmed by a venue or the quality press, so none is listed here. The port's listening is older and louder: a kompania of bouzouki, guitar and baglamas playing to a room that knows the words, often with little or no amplification. If you want to hear rebetiko properly, sit near the musicians in one of the rooms in this fold. For a vinyl room, the Athens guide has one.
